newsitem.title: FRANCE: French rainbow coalition preaches against Pope.
newsitem.headline: French rainbow coalition preaches against Pope.

text.p: Anarchists, homosexuals, rights activists and heirs to the French Revolution marched through Paris on Sunday in an unholy alliance against Pope John Paul as he celebrated a pagan king on the last day of a visit to France.

While some 200,000 faithful attended the papal mass in Reims, northeast of the capital, some 3,000 oddly-assorted demonstrators rallied to defend the secular Republic and denounce his teachings on contraception and abortion.
Marchers sported blown-up condoms tied to their hair, others brandished caricatures of the Pontiff, and one tall, lanky man dressed up as a nun with his face plastered in white powder.
A doctored photograph showed the Pope making a rude gesture with his right arm below the caption "Religion Oppresses".

"We're here to demonstrate against the state spending money on the visit and against the moral order he preaches on abortion and condoms," said Hughes Lenoir of the Anarchists Federation, among the biggest groups in the rally.

Militant activists of the Act-Up homosexual movement blew whistles and sounded horns. "The Pope says that gays mustn't live their homosexuality. That's why we're here," said a member of the SOS Homophobia group.

France's historical church-state divide drew the broadest support, with many demonstrators sporting the red bonnets typical of 1789 revolutionaries as they marched on the site of the Bastille fortress which was razed after the Revolution.

"The far-right and the government have hijacked the baptism of (Frankish king) Clovis. The Pope let himself be manoeuvred, Clovis was a thug," said Renee Lemignot of the Movement Against Racism (MRAP).
Anti-papal activists see Clovis, whose baptism 1,500 years ago was the focus of the Reims celebration, as a Dark Ages warlord who converted out of political convenience, not faith.
State and local authority spending of an estimated 30 million francs ($6 million) on facilities for the visit also raised hackles at the march, punctuated by songs dating from the Revolution.
"My red bonnet represents the true Republic, the legacy of the Revolution," said Albert Bailliot, denouncing the state funds as a violation of the separation of church and state.
Earlier, freemasons visited the site of the 1792 Valmy battlefield near Reims to mark the downfall of the monarchy and the proclamation of the Republic.
Freemasons believe the Pope's marking the Clovis anniversary tramples the ideals of the Revolution, violates a 1905 law separating the state from the Church and plays into the hands of the far-right.

"Churches are trying under various forms to impose fundamentalism...oppose women's rights, impose the (Moslem) veil, to let themselves be recognised as a component of Europe," Yves Lapouge, head of the French freemasons, told supporters in an attack on both Roman Catholicism and Islam.

In a statement, he far-right and anti-immigrant National Front defiantly branded the Clovis baptism "an event of a high spiritual significance" and dismissed anti-Pope protests as the work of "proponents of moral laxity and the decay of France".
Atheists also held a protest rally in a sports hall in Reims, where Clovis was baptised and where French kings were traditionally crowned. Police said some 700 people attended.
